title: .NET platform vs runtime vs SDK vs framework and alternatives
concepts: A programming language, its compiler, the runtime that executes compiled programs, reusable libraries, developer tools, and application frameworks solve related but different problems. The .NET platform brings these parts together; understanding the boundaries helps explain build, run, deploy, and compatibility behavior.

The .NET SDK contains build and development tools and includes runtime components, while a runtime installation is intended to execute applications. An installed SDK can target multiple frameworks; the runtime selected at execution is a separate decision from the target framework recorded by a project.

A target framework moniker (TFM) selects the API contract used at build and package-compatibility time. It does not by itself guarantee that every operating system or device can run the application; platform-specific target frameworks and runtime identifiers add different constraints.

Modern .NET is Microsoft's primary, open-source, cross-platform implementation. .NET Framework remains a Windows implementation in maintenance for existing applications. .NET Standard is an API specification for library compatibility, not a runtime or a replacement for modern .NET.

Comparable platforms such as Java, Node.js, Python, Go, and Rust package languages, tooling, runtime behavior, libraries, deployment, and support differently. Choose by workload, hosting environment, ecosystem, performance needs, team skills, interoperability, and lifecycle rather than by language syntax alone.

versionNotes.edition: .NET 5-11 platform naming and current support checked 2026-11-20
items: .NET 5 unified the product naming after .NET Core 3.1: modern cross-platform releases use the simple .NET name, while .NET Framework remains a distinct Windows implementation. As checked on 2026-11-20, .NET 11 is the current STS release and .NET 10 is the current LTS release; both are supported until November 2028. .NET Standard is a frozen API specification and remains relevant mainly when a library needs a shared API contract across implementation families; new applications generally target a specific modern .NET release.

scopeExclusions: C# syntax, source-file structure, and entry points are taught in t01-002; this topic only names the compiler and build chain to show platform boundaries.
The exact .NET CLI command and MSBuild property inventories belong to a dedicated tooling topic; this overview introduces only the major roles and selection decisions.
ASP.NET Core, Windows desktop, mobile, and web-framework APIs have dedicated topics; this manifest compares application stacks without duplicating their API inventories.
Runtime internals, JIT and AOT details, assembly loading, and reflection are covered in t01-019.
This is a decision-oriented comparison, not a complete tutorial for Java, JavaScript, Python, Go, or Rust APIs.
